content: Tonicity refers to the effective osmolarity or osmolality of a solution in relation to a specific membrane. While osmolarity and osmolality are intrinsic properties of a solution, tonicity is defined by how a solution interacts with a membrane. It is determined by the concentration of solutes that can exert an osmotic force across the membrane. Importantly, tonicity is influenced by the permeability of solutes; solutes that can cross the membrane (permeant solutes) do not contribute to tonicity, whereas solutes that cannot cross the membrane (impermeant solutes) do. Tonicity is categorized into three types: hypertonicity, isotonicity, and hypotonicity. Hypertonicity In a hypertonic environment, the concentration of impermeable solutes outside the cell is higher than inside the cell. In animal cells, this process results in a phenomenon called crenation, where the cell becomes distorted and wrinkled due to water loss. Some organisms have developed mechanisms to cope with hypertonic environments. For instance, saltwater fish live in a hypertonic environment because seawater contains a higher concentration of solutes than their internal fluids. To counteract osmotic water loss, these fish drink large amounts of seawater and excrete excess salt through specialized mechanisms, a process known as osmoregulation. In plant cells, the effects of hypertonicity are more pronounced. As water exits the cell, the cell membrane detaches from the rigid cell wall, except at points where it remains connected to adjacent cells via structures called plasmodesmata. This condition, known as plasmolysis, gives the cell a pincushion-like appearance, and the plasmodesmata become so constricted that their function is nearly lost. Isotonicity In an isotonic environment, the concentration of impermeable solutes is equal on both sides of the cell membrane. This equilibrium results in no net movement of water into or out of the cell. This state of balance is what cells in hypertonic or hypotonic environments strive to achieve. Hypotonicity A hypotonic environment is the opposite of a hypertonic one. In this case, the concentration of impermeable solutes is higher inside the cell than outside. As a result, water moves into the cell. In animal cells, this influx of water causes the cells to swell, and if the water intake continues unchecked, the cells may eventually burst (lyse). Plant cells, however, are protected from bursting by their rigid cell walls, which provide structural reinforcement and limit excessive expansion.
